Expectation1: Meet sales targets set by management
Situation1: Midway through the week, their individual sales numbers are already on pace to surpass the quota.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I stared at my computer screen, the sales dashboard glowing with numbers that told me I was on track to crush my quota this week. My manager’s words echoed in my mind: “Keep up the momentum, don’t let up.” I could almost feel the pat on the back, the promise of a bonus. But then my phone buzzed—a message from the advocacy group. There’d been an incident, something ugly and urgent, and they needed someone to draft a statement, organize a response, get the word out now. My heart pounded. I knew the power of a well-timed campaign, how it could shift public opinion, maybe even policy. But every minute I spent on advocacy was a minute not spent dialing leads, not closing deals. I could hear my manager’s disappointment already, see the dip in my numbers if I paused. Yet, the faces of those affected by the discrimination haunted me. I felt pulled in two, the pressure to perform and the need to speak out both tightening around me, demanding I choose.
